payload.source_label: Equation (1.8): q_t + f(q)_x = 0 with flux function f

contract.statement: Equation (1.8) presents a one-dimensional homogeneous conservation law: the time derivative of q plus the spatial derivative of its flux f(q) equals zero, with f identified as the flux function [printed p. 3, Section 1.1, (1.8) and following sentence]. The inherited unknown q is vector-valued, so one-dimensional concerns space rather than the number of conserved components [printed p. 1, paragraph following (1.1); printed p. 4, opening paragraph]. This passage specifies the equation's form rather than claiming that arbitrary functions satisfy it or asserting existence and uniqueness [printed p. 3, introduction to (1.8)]. The source separately qualifies derivation of this differential form from the integral conservation law by sufficient smoothness and acknowledges discontinuous solutions [printed p. 4, Section 1.1.2].
assumptions: The displayed equation concerns one spatial dimension and a homogeneous conservation law. [Printed p. 3, Section 1.1, introductory sentences and (1.8).]

For a classical differential interpretation, the displayed partial derivatives must exist; this is an analyst inference from (1.8). The source explicitly requires sufficient smoothness of q and f(q) when deriving (1.8) from the integral form, without specifying a precise regularity class. [Printed p. 3, (1.8); printed p. 4, Section 1.1.2, opening paragraph.]

The chapter studies time-dependent first-order systems, and Section 1.1 places conservation laws in the discussion of homogeneous hyperbolic equations. [Printed p. 1, introduction preceding (1.1); printed p. 3, Section 1.1 opening.]

The nearby hyperbolicity criterion concerns the flux Jacobian f′(q): the previously stated matrix conditions are real eigenvalues and m linearly independent eigenvectors. These conditions describe hyperbolicity in the surrounding discussion; they are not additional terms in equation (1.8). [Printed p. 3, opening paragraph and sentence following (1.9).]
Both linear flux f(q)=Aq and flux nonlinear in q occur within the conservation-law discussion. [Printed p. 4, opening paragraph.]

The source distinguishes the differential form from an integral form and explicitly acknowledges discontinuous solutions for which the smooth derivation does not apply. [Printed p. 4, Sections 1.1.1–1.1.2.]
quantifiers: Inherited notation: x ∈ ℝ is the single spatial variable and t ∈ ℝ is time; q : ℝ × ℝ → ℝᵐ is the unknown with m components. Equation (1.8) does not repeat these declarations or give explicit quantifiers. [Printed p. 1, paragraph surrounding (1.1); printed p. 3, (1.8).]

f is the flux function of the state q. Its vector-valued interpretation and compatible input/output dimensions follow from the vector q, the addition in (1.8), and the Jacobian matrix in (1.9); an explicit function-type declaration for f is not supplied. [Printed p. 3, (1.8)–(1.9); printed p. 4, opening paragraph.]
